title: Marshall Field & Co. v. Clark (1892)
summary: The Court upheld reciprocal-tariff authority as execution of Congress’s policy, while a separate opinion treated the President’s evaluative choices as legislative.
notes:
Justice Harlan wrote for the Court and, quoting the Ohio Supreme Court, stated the governing line verbatim: "The true distinction ... is between the delegation of power to make the law, which necessarily involves a discretion as to what it shall be, and conferring authority or discretion as to its execution, to be exercised under and in pursuance of the law."

The same decision announced the enrolled-bill rule: a bill signed by the Speaker and President of the Senate and approved by the President is conclusive evidence of its passage, so courts will not look behind it to the journals.

sections.Parties: Marshall Field & Co. and other importers challenged customs assessments collected by federal customs officials. Their constitutional attack concerned the validity of the 1890 Tariff Act.
sections.Material Facts: The Act allowed designated products to enter duty-free but required the President to suspend that treatment when he found foreign duties or exactions reciprocally unequal and unreasonable. Congress listed the replacement duties, including detailed sugar rates, but left the President to assess foreign treatment and determine the suspension’s duration. The importers contended that this authority transferred legislative power and invalidated the law underlying their assessments.
sections.Procedural History: Customs collectors imposed duties, the Board of General Appraisers approved the assessments, and the federal circuit courts affirmed. The Supreme Court upheld the challenged legislation. Justice Lamar, joined by Chief Justice Fuller, concurred in the judgments but disagreed with the Court’s conclusion that the reciprocity provision was constitutional.
sections.Issue: Did Congress delegate legislative power by authorizing the President to find unequal foreign trade treatment and activate specified tariff consequences?
sections.Holding: The Court held that the provision did not transfer legislative power. Congress made the policy and fixed the duties; the President ascertained the contingency and executed the statutory direction.
sections.Reasoning: The majority relied on Brig Aurora and a long history of trade statutes conferring executive discretion. It read the direction as obligatory once the President found the triggering condition. In its account, Congress had already decided the expediency of reciprocity and the duties to impose; presidential judgment concerned implementation. Lamar’s opinion distinguished genuinely contingent legislation from this statute’s authority to decide what trade treatment was unreasonable and how long a suspension was just. He therefore treated the evaluative breadth as a legislative choice. The disagreement exposes the difficulty of separating fact-finding from policy judgment even where Congress specifies the eventual rates.

topics.lrs-s-conditional-legislation: The majority treated reciprocal inequality as a fact triggering Congress’s tariffs; the separate opinion regarded the same assessment as a policy choice.
topics.lrs-s-intelligible-principle: Field's execution/legislation distinction is the precursor that Hampton reformulated as the intelligible-principle test.
